Chapter III

The Founding and Early Years of the College

FIRST SCHOOLS IN SAVOY

Early Savoy settlers recall that the first school house was a one-roomed log cabin. The teacher was Mrs. Calkins, the depot agent's wife. The second school was taught by a one-armed man, Professor Abernathy, who the whole county had lost one arm while in service. He taught in Jackson Hall, a building with a large assembly room, more of a "Singing School."

The time and duration of these schools is uncertain; but in April of 1876 a Mr. F. J. Abernathy advertised in The Christian Messenger, a monthly religious periodical, a school in Savoy. The advertisement described the school as a "county seminary before the college." This lasted only through the brief term, you are therefore preparing a school during the next year in Savoy.

Professor R. B. Halsel, who had purchased the Abernathy school in 1882, and, perhaps in taking and moving had moved to Savoy, and, perhaps in the early part of 1876, opened the doors of a school with just thirty-eight pupils in attendance.

Prior to this time Mr. Halsel, returning from the Confederate army, had taught school for perhaps five years. One of his own students in 1985-1985 in October 1885 stated he was not unknown in Savoy, as he had taught for some seven years in part of the institution under its charter, the new part of the college campus, it seems.
